content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

1	In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
6	
7	The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.
8	
9	The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
10	
11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. 26	
27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.
30

Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.
32

35	A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.
38	
39	Mechanical exposure indicator
40	
41	The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.
42	
43	The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.
44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. 52	
53	Essential and optional features

Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

57	The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

I traced each of the following to an exact affirmative passage: insulated outer shell / removable product tray / removable thermal module / insulated lid; tray on feet with a lower return passage beneath; tray side walls spaced inward from shell side walls forming two side supply passages; rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes, resting above the tray and below the lid; central inlet opening; two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes; peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages; the full circulation sequence (rise -> central inlet -> divide along cassette faces -> descend guide ducts -> side supply passages -> tray perforations -> lower return passage); absence of fan, pump or powered air mover; depending indexing rib on the lid entering a mating channel and shifting the module into a registered position with outlet/supply-passage overlap; compressible lid gasket sealing against the shell upper edge after registration; resilient spacer-frame feet pressed against shell ledges by the same closing movement so the module cannot lift away during transport; shallow condensate channel around the tray with a removable absorbent wick; discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts; pull tab accessible with the tray removed so the wick is replaced without opening a cassette; mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside with stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position surviving cassette recovery, manual reset only after opening, and no control of airflow; and the assembly/use sequence supporting method claims 17-20. Claim 5 (cassettes removable from the frame) traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"; claims 4 and 15 (confronting inner faces across a central space; upwardly opening mating channel) are necessary implications of "two opposed phase-change cassettes", the downward-dividing central inlet and a depending rib entering from above; claim 12 (rib meets channel while the lid is still spaced above the shell) is the necessary implication of the gasket sealing "after registration". Optional-feature designation for the wick and indicator matches "The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features."

Text checks: claims and description use the same terms and relationships; every numeral in numerals.md is used in the description and appears on at least one figure, and each numeral denotes exactly one part; claim antecedent basis is complete throughout claims 1-20; there is no means-plus-function language; the three statutory classes and the dependent-claim ladder match the brief; title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research); the abstract is a single paragraph of about 141 words. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains anywhere in draft/ or figures/. No text anywhere adds an "by way of example" or "any closed outline" style embodiment to justify a renderer's shape choice - the description's only generality is the ordinary closing boilerplate, which asserts no shape.

Section-line consistency (the named v9 check) passes: the only named section line is 7-7. FIG-6.md draws it as a horizontal broken line whose two ends each carry an arrow and the repeated designation 7 ("the repeated section designation 7 at the two ends makes the cutting-plane line read line 7-7"), FIG-7.md is "taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6", and 07-drawings.md uses the identical designation in both entries ("carrying the line 7-7 on which FIG. 7 is taken" / "taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6"). Both arrows point the same way, and FIG. 7's left-outer / right-inner wall orientation is consistent with that viewing direction. FIG. 1's plane is described verbally and names no line, so no repeated designation is owed.

Findings are five minor items, all confined to the figure briefs or to the Brief Description, none of which propagates into the claims or reaches claim scope: (1) FIG. 1's enlargement curves do not enclose everything the enlarged views show - FIG. 4 shows the lower return passage 24 and FIG. 5 shows the pull tab 74, neither of which is within, or even depicted in, the FIG. 1 regions those curves are said to enclose; (2) FIG. 1 asserts a count of two tray feet where the inventor said only "feet"; (3) FIG. 2 gives the cassettes a proportion ("running most of the frame length") that the disclosure does not state; (4) FIG. 7 gives the spring a coil form surrounding the indicator stem, a topology/contact relationship the disclosure does not state and which is not tagged "shown schematically" as the neighbouring generic elements are; (5) FIGS. 6 and 7 illustrate the indicator stem in the exposed position, but neither the Brief Description nor the detailed description identifies the state shown. findings.title: FIG. 1 enlargement curves do not enclose (and FIG. 1 does not depict) everything FIGS. 4 and 5 show
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md (broken-line curve list); cross-checked against figures/FIG-4.md, figures/FIG-5.md and draft/07-drawings.md
findings.detail: An enlarged view must show the structure inside the region the parent view marks. FIG-1.md says the lower-left curve is drawn "around the left outboard channel opening, left gap and tray openings", but FIG. 4 additionally shows the tray bottom wall and the lower return passage 24 ("the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24"), and 07-drawings.md states FIG. 4 shows "the lower return passage". Likewise the lower-right curve is drawn "around the right channel lower end, its downward opening, the right trough and absorbent body", yet FIG. 5 shows the pull tab 74 ("A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface... This strip is the pull tab 74") and 07-drawings.md states FIG. 5 shows "the absorbent wick and its pull tab" - FIG. 1 never depicts a pull tab at all. The upper-left curve list likewise omits the compressible body that FIG. 3 shows as the lid gasket 64. This is a figure-to-figure inconsistency only; the structures themselves are all inventor-supported.
findings.evidence: FIG-1.md: "one at the lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap and tray openings; and one at the lower right around the right channel lower end, its downward opening, the right trough and absorbent body." vs FIG-4.md: "the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24" and FIG-5.md: "This strip is the pull tab 74."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-1.md, add a pull tab to the depiction and extend the curve contents: change the trough sentence to "A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body, a narrow strip rising from the upper surface of the right-hand body into the gap."; change the curve list to "one at the upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, the compressible body on that top end, the left inward-projecting block and the small block on it; one at the lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap, tray openings, the tray bottom wall and the space beneath it; and one at the lower right around the right channel lower end, its downward opening, the right trough, the absorbent body and the narrow strip rising from it."

findings.title: FIG. 1 asserts a count of two tray feet that the disclosure does not give
findings.detail: The brief states the tray stands "on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22", which reads as the complete set of feet. The inventor disclosed feet without any count or appearance. FIG-2.md handles the analogous problem correctly for the resilient feet by hedging ("two visible at the front, shown schematically"); FIG. 1 does not. A count is technical substance and is not covered by the generic-outline depiction convention.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "standing above the floor 12 on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22" (figures/FIG-1.md). Nearest source, showing the gap: "The product tray is suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray." (input/disclosure.md) - no count and no shape is given.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-1.md, replace "standing above the floor 12 on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22" with "standing above the floor 12 on short hatched blocks, two of them appearing in this section, shown schematically, these blocks being the tray feet 22".

findings.title: FIG. 2 gives the phase-change cassettes an unsupported proportion relative to the spacer frame
findings.detail: The brief specifies that each cassette runs "most of the frame length". The disclosure states only that the spacer frame holds "two opposed phase-change cassettes" and gives no dimension, extent or proportion for them relative to the frame. A proportion conveys technical substance and is expressly outside the generic-outline depiction convention, even though the slab shape itself is properly tagged "shown schematically".
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length." (figures/FIG-2.md). Nearest source, showing the gap: "The thermal module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes." (input/disclosure.md) - no extent or proportion is stated.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-2.md, delete the proportion: replace "each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length" with "each parallel to the long side walls, their extent along the frame shown schematically".

findings.title: FIG. 7 gives the spring a coil form surrounding the indicator stem, a topology the disclosure does not state
findings.detail: The brief specifies a coil spring that "surrounds the shaft" - a contact/topology relationship between two named parts. The disclosure says only that "a spring moves the indicator stem". Unlike the indicator body 80 and the latch 84 in the same brief, the spring is not tagged "shown schematically", so the coil-around-the-stem arrangement reads as a disclosed structure rather than as a drawing convention. No change to the description or claims is needed; both remain generic ("a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position").
findings.evidence: Candidate: "A coil spring surrounds the shaft within the outline, drawn as aligned loops and shown extended, its loops spaced apart. This spring is the spring 86." (figures/FIG-7.md). Nearest source, showing the gap: "If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position." (input/disclosure.md) - no spring type, form or mounting is given.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-7.md, replace that sentence with "A spring, shown schematically as a coil of aligned loops within the outline and drawn extended, acts on the shaft in the direction of its outward projection. This spring is the spring 86."

findings.title: FIGS. 6 and 7 depict the indicator in the exposed position, but no text says which state is illustrated
findings.where: draft/07-drawings.md (FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 entries); draft/08-detailed-description.md, Mechanical exposure indicator section; figures/FIG-6.md and figures/FIG-7.md
findings.detail: Both figure briefs specify "with the indicator stem in the exposed position", and FIG. 6 accordingly shows the stem end projecting outward. The Brief Description and the detailed description never identify the illustrated state; the detailed description instead introduces the stem as "movable between a stowed position and an exposed position" retained by the latch, leaving the reader unable to tell which condition the drawings show. The exposed position is fully inventor-supported, so the cure is a text statement, not a figure change.
findings.evidence: figures/FIG-6.md: "with the indicator stem in the exposed position"; figures/FIG-7.md: "with the indicator stem in the exposed position". draft/07-drawings.md: "FIG. 6 is a fragmentary elevation... showing the indicator visible from outside the carrier and the outer end of the indicator stem" - state unstated. Source: "a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position" (input/disclosure.md).
findings.fix: In draft/07-drawings.md, append ", the indicator stem being shown in the exposed position" to the FIG. 6 entry (after "the outer end of the indicator stem") and to the FIG. 7 entry (after "the temperature-responsive latch and the spring"). In draft/08-detailed-description.md, after "The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.", add "FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position."
